app.name: Brick Shop
app.title: Brick Shop: learn JavaScript and the DOM

editor.label: Code editor
editor.htmlFixed: The page is fixed in every step: read it to know what to select, and write your code in script.js.

console.title: Console
console.empty: Nothing logged yet. Try `console.log('hello')` in your code.

notices.formReload: The form was sent and the page reloaded: your code ran again from the start. Call `event.preventDefault()` in the submit listener to stay on the page.

errors.infiniteLoop: This loop never ends: it was stopped after {{count}} turns. Check its condition.

variables.name: variables
variables.definition: A named box that holds a value. `const` creates one that never gets a new value, `let` one that can change later: `let count = 0` then `count = count + 1`.

types.name: types
types.definition: Every value has a type: `number` (12, 0.5), `string` (text between quotes, '12'), `boolean` (true, false), and more. `typeof` tells you which one. With a string, `+` glues text instead of adding numbers.

conditions.name: if / else
conditions.definition: `if (condition) { … } else { … }` runs the first block when the condition is true, the second one otherwise. Compare with `===`, `!==`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`.

querySelector.name: querySelector
querySelector.definition: `document.querySelector(selector)` returns the first element matching a CSS selector (`#id`, `.class`, `.card .name`), or `null`. Its `textContent` is the text inside it: read it or give it a new value.

classList.name: classList
classList.definition: The list of classes of an element. `add`, `remove` and `toggle` change it, `contains` tells whether a class is there. The page's CSS gives each class its look.

loops.name: for
loops.definition: `for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { … }` runs the block again and again: start, condition checked before every turn, step after every turn.

querySelectorAll.name: querySelectorAll
querySelectorAll.definition: `document.querySelectorAll(selector)` returns every element matching the selector, in page order. Go through them with `for (const el of list) { … }`; `list.length` counts them.

functions.name: function
functions.definition: A named piece of code you can call again and again. It receives values as parameters and gives one back with `return`: `function double(n) { return n * 2 }`.

map.name: map
map.definition: `array.map((item) => …)` builds a new array of the same length, with what the function returns for each item. The original array is not changed.

filter.name: filter
filter.definition: `array.filter((item) => …)` builds a new array with only the items for which the function returns true.

find.name: find
find.definition: `array.find((item) => …)` returns the first item for which the function returns true, or `undefined` when there is none.

addEventListener.name: addEventListener
addEventListener.definition: `element.addEventListener('click', () => { … })` runs the function every time the event happens on the element, not right away. Common events: `click`, `input`, `submit`, `keydown`.

localStorage.name: localStorage
localStorage.definition: Text saved by the browser for the site, still there after a reload. `localStorage.setItem(key, value)` saves, `localStorage.getItem(key)` reads (or returns `null`).

FormData.name: FormData
FormData.definition: `new FormData(form)` reads every field of a form at once; `data.get('name')` returns the value of the field whose `name` attribute is `name`.

shop-sign.title: Name your shop
intro: Welcome to the Brick Shop! In every step you get a small web page and make it work with JavaScript. Your code goes in `script.js` on the left; the page and the console are on the right.
First, the sign is blank. A variable keeps a value under a name: `const shopName = 'My shop'`. The last two lines already put the variables on the sign.
shop-sign.goal: Give `shopName` and `city` a value so the sign shows the name of your shop and its city.
hints: Text values are written between quotes: `'Brick Shop'`.
Only change what is between the quotes of `''`: the rest already works.
shop-sign.recap: `const` keeps a value under a name. The page uses the name, so changing the value in one place changes the page.

checks.named: The sign shows a shop name

intro: The shop has 12 red bricks and 8 blue ones, but the total says 128. Look at the console: `blueBricks` is a `string`, text that happens to contain digits.
With a string, `+` glues texts together: `12 + '8'` gives `'128'`. `Number('8')` turns the text into the number 8.
brick-count.goal: Make the total show 20, keeping `blueBricks` as the text `'8'`.
hints: The problem is in the line that computes `total`.
Convert `blueBricks` before adding it.
brick-count.recap: Values have types. Text read from a page or a form is a `string`: convert it with `Number()` before doing maths.

price-tag.title: The price tag
intro: Gluing texts with `+` quickly gets messy. A template literal is written between backticks instead of quotes, and inserts values with `${…}`. The example in the hints shows one.
Inside `${…}` you can write any expression, maths included: `${price * 2}`.
price-tag.goal: Show `4 × Red brick = 2 €` in the summary, with a template literal built from the three variables.
hints: Backticks are not quotes: on most keyboards, the key is next to Enter or 1.
The total is `quantity * price`.
price-tag.recap: Template literals mix text and values with `${…}`. Numbers become text on their own.

checks.usesTemplate: The code uses a template literal with `${…}`

sold-out.title: Sold out?
intro: The badge always says In stock, even when there is nothing left. The code must decide: that's what `if` is for.
`if (stock === 0) { … } else { … }` runs the first block when the stock is 0, the second one otherwise. `===` compares two values.
sold-out.goal: Show `Sold out` when the stock is 0, and `In stock` otherwise.
hints: The condition goes between parentheses: `stock === 0`.
Put one `status.textContent = …` line in each block.
sold-out.recap: `if` and `else` choose between two pieces of code. The checks run your code with several stocks: it must work for all of them.

checks.soldOut: With a stock of 0, the badge says `Sold out`
checks.inStock: With a stock of 7, the badge says `In stock`

almost-gone.title: Almost gone
intro: Shoppers like to know when a brick is about to run out. Between the two cases, add a third one with `else if`.
Conditions are read from top to bottom and only the first true one runs: put the most specific case first.
almost-gone.goal: Show `Sold out` at 0, `Almost gone` from 1 to 4, and `In stock` from 5.
hints: `else if (stock < 5) { … }` goes between the `if` block and the `else` block.
A stock of 0 is also below 5: that's why the `stock === 0` test must come first.
almost-gone.recap: `else if` adds as many cases as needed. Order matters: the first true condition wins.

featured.title: Brick of the week
intro: `document.querySelector` takes the same selectors as CSS: `#banner` for an id, `.card` for a class, `.featured .name` for a `.name` inside a `.featured`.
It returns the first matching element. Open `index.html` to see the page: the featured card is the second one, and its name and price are empty.
featured.goal: Write the name and the price of the featured card, without touching the other cards.
hints: `document.querySelector('.name')` returns the first name of the page, the red brick's: you need a more precise selector.
Select the `.name` and the `.price` inside `.featured`, then set their `textContent`.
featured.recap: `querySelector` + `textContent` is the base of DOM changes: select precisely, then write.

spotlight.title: Spring sale
intro: The page's CSS hides any element with the `hidden` class and frames any card with the `highlight` class. Changing classes changes the look.
`element.classList.add('x')` adds a class, `element.classList.remove('x')` removes one, and the other classes stay.
spotlight.goal: Show the sale banner and highlight the yellow card.
hints: The variables `banner` and `yellowCard` already hold the elements.
Avoid `className = …`: it replaces every class, and the card would lose its `card` class.
spotlight.recap: `classList` changes one class at a time. The style stays in the CSS, the JavaScript only switches classes.

checks.bannerShown: The banner is visible and keeps its `banner` class
checks.highlighted: The yellow card has the `highlight` class
checks.keepsCard: The yellow card keeps its `card` class
checks.onlyYellow: The other cards are not highlighted

sold-out-badge.title: On or off
intro: The `sold-out` class greys a card out. The page may come with the class already there, or not: your code must leave it in the right state either way.
`classList.toggle('sold-out', condition)` adds the class when the condition is true and removes it when it's false.
sold-out-badge.goal: The card has the `sold-out` class when its stock is 0, and only then.
hints: Without a second argument, `toggle` flips the class: a card that already had it would lose it.
The condition is the same as in the previous steps: `stock === 0`.
sold-out-badge.recap: `toggle(name, condition)` keeps a class in line with a condition, whatever the starting state.

checks.addsWhenEmpty: Stock 0, no class yet: the card becomes sold out
checks.removesWhenRestocked: Stock 6, class already there: the card is available again
checks.staysSoldOut: Stock 0, class already there: the card stays sold out
checks.staysAvailable: Stock 6, no class: the card stays available

countdown.title: Countdown
intro: New bricks are on their way. Writing `5 4 3 2 1` by hand works, but a loop repeats the work for you.
`for (let i = 5; i >= 1; i--) { … }` starts at 5, runs while `i` is at least 1, and takes 1 away after every turn.
countdown.goal: Show `5 4 3 2 1 Go!` by adding each number to `text` in a loop.
hints: Inside the loop, add the number and a space: `text = text + i + ' '`.
A loop that never stops is stopped for you: check that `i` goes towards the end of the condition.
countdown.recap: A `for` loop has a start, a condition and a step. Counting down works just like counting up.

cart-total.title: The cart total
intro: `document.querySelectorAll('.price')` returns every price of the cart, not only the first one.
Go through the list with `for (const price of prices) { … }`: on each turn, `price` is the next element.
cart-total.goal: Show the sum of every price of the cart in the total.
hints: The text of an element is a string: convert it with `Number(price.textContent)`.
Add each price to `total` inside the loop: `total = total + …`.
cart-total.recap: `querySelectorAll` and `for...of` treat many elements the same way. The checks try another cart: the code must not depend on the number of items.

checks.otherCart: With another cart, the total is right too (`6.5`)

sold-out-cards.title: Empty shelves
intro: The loop over the cards is ready, and it already reads each card's stock. `card.querySelector('.count')` searches inside that card only.
Combine what you know: a loop, a condition and `classList`.
sold-out-cards.goal: Every card with a stock of 0 gets the `sold-out` class, the others don't.
hints: Inside the loop, test `stock === 0`.
Add the class to `card`, the card of the current turn.
sold-out-cards.recap: Loop + condition + class is the shape of most page updates: go through elements and change the ones that match.

checks.emptyMarked: Only the two empty cards are sold out
checks.otherShelf: On another shelf, the right cards are sold out too

format-price.title: Two decimals
intro: Prices show up as `0.5` or `2`. A function writes the rule once and applies it everywhere: the loop already calls `formatPrice` for every price.
`(0.5).toFixed(2)` gives the text `'0.50'`, with exactly two decimals.
format-price.goal: Make `formatPrice(amount)` return the price with two decimals and ` €`, like `2.00 €`.
hints: Only the line `return amount` needs to change.
Glue `' €'` after `amount.toFixed(2)`.
format-price.recap: A function takes parameters and gives a result back with `return`. The checks call it directly, so it must work for any amount.

checks.pricesOnPage: Every price of the page has two decimals and €

stock-label.title: One rule, many cards
intro: The stock rule from step 5 is needed on every card. Put it in a function that receives the stock and returns the label.
`return` ends the function right away: after a `return` inside an `if`, the rest is skipped.
stock-label.goal: Make `stockLabel(stock)` return `Sold out`, `Almost gone` or `In stock`.
hints: Start with `if (stock === 0) { return 'Sold out' }`.
Thanks to `return`, you don't need `else`: the last line returns `'In stock'`.
stock-label.recap: A function turns a rule into a reusable tool. The loop calls it for each card, the checks call it with any stock.

catalog.title: The catalog
intro: The catalog is now an array of objects. Each brick has a `name`, a `color`, a `price` and a `stock`: `brick.name` reads one of them.
`bricks.map((brick) => brick.name)` returns a new array with what the arrow function returns for each brick.
catalog.goal: Show the name of every brick, then every price followed by ` €`.
hints: Replace `[]` with a call to `bricks.map(...)`.
For the prices, the function returns `brick.price + ' €'`.
catalog.recap: `map` transforms every item of an array into something else, and always keeps the same number of items.

checks.names: The names of the five bricks are shown
checks.prices: The five prices are shown with €

red-only.title: Only the red ones
intro: `filter` keeps some items of an array: those for which the function returns true. The result can be shorter than the original.
`bricks.filter((brick) => brick.price < 1)` keeps the bricks cheaper than 1 €.
red-only.goal: List the red bricks only, and count the bricks that are in stock.
hints: For the red bricks, the condition is `brick.color === 'red'`.
A brick is in stock when `brick.stock > 0`.
red-only.recap: `filter` keeps the items that pass a test. Chain it with `map` to show only what you need.

checks.redOnly: The list shows `Red brick, Red door`

find-brick.title: Find a brick
intro: The search field holds a brick name. `find` returns the first item for which the function returns true: one brick, not an array.
When nothing matches, `find` returns `undefined`, and the `else` block shows Not found.
find-brick.goal: Find the brick whose name is the text of the search field, and show its price.
hints: Compare each brick's `name` with `wanted`.
`bricks.find((brick) => brick.name === wanted)`
find-brick.recap: `find` returns one item or `undefined`. Always plan for the case where nothing is found.

checks.blueRoof: With `Blue roof`, the result is `Blue roof: 1.2 €`
checks.otherBrick: With `Green plate`, the result is `Green plate: 2 €`
checks.notFound: With an unknown name, the result is `Not found`

add-to-cart.title: Add to cart
intro: Until now your code ran once, when the page loaded. `addEventListener` gives the browser a function to run later, every time something happens.
`button.addEventListener('click', () => { … })` runs the block on every click. Try it in the page on the right.
add-to-cart.goal: Every click on Add to cart adds 1 to the counter of the sign.
hints: In the listener, add 1 to `count`, then write it in `counter.textContent`.
`count` is declared with `let` outside the listener, so it remembers its value between clicks.
add-to-cart.recap: An event listener reacts to the user. The variables outside of it keep the state between two events.

checks.oneClick: After one click, the cart shows 1
checks.threeClicks: After three clicks, the cart shows 3

dark-mode.title: Night mode
intro: The page has a night look: it applies when `<body>` has the `dark` class. `document.body` is the `<body>` element.
The button should switch from one theme to the other on each click, and its label should say what the next click does.
dark-mode.goal: Each click toggles the `dark` class of the body, and the button says `Light mode` in the dark theme, `Dark mode` otherwise.
hints: Without a second argument, `classList.toggle('dark')` is what you need here: it flips the class.
After the toggle, read `document.body.classList.contains('dark')` to choose the label.
dark-mode.recap: A listener can read the current state of the page (`contains`) to decide what to show.

checks.turnsDark: One click turns the page dark
checks.turnsBack: A second click turns it light again
checks.labelFollows: The button says `Light mode` in dark mode, then `Dark mode` again

remember-theme.title: See you tomorrow
intro: Reload the page and the theme is gone: variables live only as long as the page. `localStorage` keeps text in the browser, even after a reload.
Save the theme on every click, and read it when the page loads. What your code saves is shown under the console.
remember-theme.goal: Save the theme in `localStorage` under the key `theme` (`dark` or `light`), and start in dark mode when the saved theme is `dark`.
hints: In the listener, after the toggle: `localStorage.setItem('theme', dark ? 'dark' : 'light')`.
At the top, `localStorage.getItem('theme')` returns the saved text, or `null` the first time.
When the saved theme is dark, add the `dark` class and set the label to `Light mode`.
remember-theme.recap: `localStorage` saves text that survives a reload: save on change, read on load.

checks.startsLight: With nothing saved, the page starts light
checks.restores: After a click and a reload, the page is dark and the button says `Light mode`
checks.backToLight: After two clicks and a reload, the page is light again

order-form.title: Place an order
intro: Last step: the order form. When it's sent, the browser fires a `submit` event on the form, then reloads the page. `event.preventDefault()` cancels the reload.
`new FormData(form)` reads all the fields at once, and `data.get('customer')` returns the value of the field whose `name` is `customer`.
order-form.goal: On submit, stay on the page and show `Thanks Ada! 3 × Blue roof are on their way.` with the name, quantity and brick of the form.
hints: The first line of the listener is `event.preventDefault()`.
The field names are in `index.html`: `customer`, `brick` and `quantity`.
Build the sentence with a template literal and `data.get(...)`.
order-form.recap: You made a whole shop work: variables, conditions, loops, functions, arrays, events, storage and forms. That's the JavaScript of most web pages!

checks.preventsReload: Sending the form doesn't reload the page
checks.confirms: Ada's order of 3 Blue roof is confirmed
checks.otherOrder: Grace's order of 10 Red brick is confirmed
